strengths: The paper adds to the literature of biologically-inspired inference. The extension introduced is simple and elegant and allows generalizing P-VAE to dynamically trade-off performance for compute.

The experiments show that despite IP-VAE being order of magnitude more parameter efficient, they show significant improvement in terms of reconstruction error both for in- and out-of-distribution data.
The general presentation is good and the paper is easy to follow.

The core idea of the work, which is to modify VAEs to have a latent space that is dynamic and more neurally plausible, is interesting and seems to lead to nontrivial performance gains, at least on the data sets the authors tested.
The authors do a nice job reviewing relevant literature and relating their proposal to existing frameworks and models from neuroscience.
The idea of drawing connection to membrane potential dynamics is interesting.
The authors have done extensive experiments on a few real datasets, and the results seem good.
The paper is well-motivated, and the experiments are extensive.
Interesting results on the sparse features learned by iP-VAE is shown.
The topic is of interest. The goal of matching Machine learning concepts to the neuroscience literature is important.
The related work (section 2) is, in general, well written and structured.
weaknesses: The biggest limitation is the large number of test-time iterations required to perform inference on relatively simple, downsampled datasets... lacks a detailed analysis of the computational cost per iteration, and how this scales with the size of the latent space and input data.

The authors only compare performance against P-VAEs and other variants of iterative VAEs. It would be valuable to include well-tuned baselines with standard VAEs (amortized, Gaussian distributions) to better contextualize the model's performance.

In the appendix, the authors question the validity of the Poisson assumption, which is a known issue in computational/systems neuroscience. It would be valuable to move part of this discussion to the introduction to better contextualize the model's assumptions and limitations.
The authors only trained iP-VAEs on MNIST and a few other datasets; results on more and/or more complex data sets are needed to support the claims.
The authors only compare to very similar models and should also compare performance to the vanilla VAE and other types of generative models such as diffusion models.

The claim that iP-VAE learns a "compositional code that generalizes across domains" is strong but is supported only by sample reconstructions; quantitative analysis of the learned representations is needed.
The iP-VAE is fairly similar to the recently introduced P-VAE, raising a novelty issue.
Assuming a Markovian relationship between consecutive data points is questionable; usually latent variables are assumed Markovian, not observations.
The structure of the generative model is confusing; a schematic figure would help.
The iterative aspect of iP-VAE is presented as novel but there is no dynamics in the inputs; the same input is presented many times.
The claim that iP-VAE performs Bayesian posterior updates using membrane potential dynamics is an overstatement; updates occur in log-rate space and lack a spiking threshold rule.
The authors mention the possibility of including a leak term to make the model more neurally plausible, but they do not include it in any experiments.
The title claims a "prescriptive theory for brain-like inference" but the work is not prescriptive nor especially brain-like compared to other models.
It is unclear whether the approach is substantially better than other brain-like inference methods such as those using Langevin or MCMC sampling.
The claim that the work provides a "solid foundation for developing prescriptive theories in NeuroAI" is overly strong given the narrow problem setting.
The claim that iP-VAE is particularly well-suited to neuromorphic implementations is premature.
There are some citation typos (e.g., line 521, no parentheses).
Intuitively, why modeling the latent variable z_t as Poisson distribution is better than choosing it as Gaussian as in the vanilla VAE?
In the experiment section, T_test for iP-VAE is much higher than ia-VAE and sa-VAE. What's the running time comparison for training and inference on test samples?
The authors did not show the generative performance of IP-VAE, which is important for any Bayesian model of the brain.
At each time point the IP-VAE receives the ground truth image, making the superior reconstruction performance, generalization and parameter efficiency less impressive.

For generative models, the information about the data distribution is usually stored in the parameters, so it is natural that iP-VAE does not need many parameters if the ground truth samples are provided.
Some features shown in Figure 4 seem to overfit to digit-like shape; it is unclear if iP-VAE can achieve better generalization without these overfitted features.
The experimental section is hard to understand and unclear what the authors aim to convey.
The authors only measure reconstruction performance, omitting the KL-divergence regularisation term, which fails to capture the trade-off between reconstruction accuracy and regularisation.
By focusing only on reconstruction, the evaluation may reflect memorization rather than generalization or meaningful latent representation.
The compared works report ELBO or reconstruction together with KL, whereas the current paper does not, making comparisons less informative.
